answer.rationale: The incumbent has explicitly refused to reopen price, so neither renew_incumbent nor negotiate_terms can plausibly deliver the 18% cut finance demands. Memory c6's multi-year volume pricing path is also blocked by that refusal. The contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, so defer_decision is not viable—it would leave the assembly line (already at 94% committed volume, no buffer) without primary supply. Adding a second source (c3) mitigates concentration risk but does not itself cut primary unit cost enough and would split the one decision slot. Switching the primary contract to the low-cost vendor identified in c2 is the single lever that can meet the 18% target: c2 records that the switch cut unit cost sharply, onboarding was quick, and invoicing stayed accurate—directly relevant evidence for delivery risk. I am verifying c2 before committing because it is the load-bearing claim (the cost delta and onboarding speed) and my only verification slot; if the archive contradicts the summary, I would fall back to renew_incumbent on month-to-month terms (per c5's deferral precedent) to buy time rather than lock a longer commitment with a non-cooperative supplier. Downstream value risk: a 14-day transition window at 94% line utilisation means any onboarding slip hits committed volume; I flag this and would require the new vendor to guarantee first-delivery date before signing. I am spending my verification on c2 rather than c3 or c6 because the primary-supply switch is the action in play and c2 is the only memory that speaks to its feasibility.
